images.title: Bigger and smaller can mean less
images.purpose: Compares 5 × 3 with 6 × 2 as dot arrays to show that raising one number by 1 and lowering the other by 1 can make the product smaller.
images.composition: A before and after comparison: two dot arrays side by side with a small gap between them. Plain white background, lots of empty space around the main object, no scenery, no people, no extra text.
images.exact_structure: Left panel: a teal (#0072B2) array of dots in 3 rows of 5, exactly 15 dots, with the label '5 × 3 = 15' below. Right panel: an amber (#E69F00) array of dots in 2 rows of 6, exactly 12 dots, with the label '6 × 2 = 12' below. Centred beneath both panels, the label 'change = b − a − 1' and under it the label '3 − 5 − 1 = −3' in vermilion (#D55E00). Exactly 15 dots on the left and 12 dots on the right.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
images.takeaway: When a is at least b, (a + 1)(b − 1) is smaller than ab.
images.description: Compares 5 × 3 with 6 × 2 as dot arrays to show that raising one number by 1 and lowering the other by 1 can make the product smaller.

image_decisions.why: Seeing 15 dots become 12 breaks the belief that making one number bigger always raises the product.
